Rules can be based on ownership or record criteria. They are designed to grant additional access; they do not generally make access more restrictive than OWD.

01Owner-based

Shares records based on who owns them.

02Criteria-based

Shares records based on field values/criteria.

03Target audience

Users, roles, territories, or Public Groups receive access.

04Access level

The rule defines the level of shared access.

DATA ACCESS LEVELS

Think about the overall access posture before designing a sharing rule

These are conceptual access postures, not three literal OWD values. They help frame how open or selective the record model needs to be.

🌐
Public

Records are broadly available to users whose Profile and Permission Sets allow access.

Most open posture
⚖
Hybrid

The baseline remains selective, then Sharing Rules open only the records required by specific teams or functions.

Balanced, targeted access
🔒
Private

Users primarily access records they own or records opened by an explicit sharing mechanism.

Most restrictive posture
02
UNDERSTAND

Connect the security concept to effective access

01Owner-based

Shares records based on who owns them.

02Criteria-based

Shares records based on field values/criteria.

03Target audience

Users, roles, territories, or Public Groups receive access.

04Access level

The rule defines the level of shared access.

05Open, not restrict

Sharing Rules grant additional access from the baseline.

RECORD ACCESS: KEY CONSIDERATIONS

Define the rule by answering four questions

A Sharing Rule becomes easier to reason about when the source records, recipients, and access level are separated.

📄
1. Share which records?

Define the records that should be shared.

  • Owned by certain users
  • Meeting defined criteria
ExamplesOpportunities over a threshold, Accounts owned by a sales team
👥
2. From which users?

Identify the source population for the records.

  • Public Groups
  • Roles
  • Roles and Subordinates
  • Queues for supported objects
ExamplesSales Team group, Sales Manager role, Support Queue
👤
3. To which users?

Choose who should receive the additional access.

  • Public Groups
  • Roles
  • Roles and Subordinates
ExamplesAll Sales Users, Regional Managers, Partner Community group
🔐
4. What level of access?

Set the level of access granted by the rule.

  • Read Only
  • Read/Write
ExamplesRead Only for visibility, Read/Write for collaborative updates
03
INVESTIGATE

Use the right checks in the right order

01

Confirm the record actually meets the rule criteria or ownership condition.

02

Confirm the intended target group/role is correct.

03

Check the access level granted by the rule.

04

Verify group membership if a Public Group is involved.

Include everyone assigned to a selected role in the organization.

Nest supported groups to build a reusable audience without repeating members.

Automation & Execution

06.1 · LEARNING TOPIC

Order of Execution

A single record save can involve multiple automation and validation layers. Order of Execution gives you a mental model for locating the layer that changed, blocked, or extended the transaction.

TRANSACTION PATH
01
LEARN

Think in execution phases, not one visible save

01
✎
User action / record save

A record is created or updated and the transaction begins.

→
02
⚡
Before the commit

Before-save FlowSalesforce Flow is declarative automation built from connected visual elements. Click to open the glossary. can update the record, while other transaction logic can also participate.

→
03
✓
Transaction checks

Apex TriggerAn Apex trigger is custom code that runs in response to record events. Click to open the glossary., Validation RulesA validation rule blocks a save when its formula evaluates to TRUE. Click to open the glossary., duplicate logic, and other automation can influence the result.

→
04
↗
After-save behavior

Automation can create related records, update other data, send notifications, or call additional processes.

→
05
◷
Post-commit work

Asynchronous activity can continue even after the visible save appears complete.

Investigation lens

Use the timing and symptom to narrow the layer. An automatic field change does not prove that Flow was responsible.

02
UNDERSTAND

Connect the symptom to the execution phase

BEFORE SAVEThe same record changes immediately

Look for logic that can modify the record before commit, including before-save automation.

SAVE BLOCKEDThe user cannot save

Inspect validation, required data, duplicate handling, permissions, and other transaction logic.

AFTER SAVEAnother record or action changes

Investigate after-save automation and downstream processes.

LATERSomething happens after the save completes

Consider post-commit or asynchronous processing and collect runtime evidence.

03
INVESTIGATE

Trace where the observed behavior could have started

1Reproduce the action

Identify the exact save, update, create, or delete operation.

2Describe the timing

Did the failure happen before save, during save, immediately after, or later?

3List possible layers

Flow, trigger, validation, duplicate logic, and downstream automation can coexist.

4Follow evidence

Use runtime information instead of disabling random automation.

04
APPLY

Use execution order to avoid the wrong assumption

PRACTICE SCENARIO

An Opportunity is saved and another field changes automatically.

Do not label the behavior “a Flow issue” yet. First identify when the value changed, what automation is configured for that event, and which layer actually performed the update.

Save→Timing→Automation layer→Evidence

Flow Types

Flow types mainly differ by what starts them and whether they interact directly with a user. Identifying the type tells you where to begin the investigation.

TRIGGER MODEL
01
LEARN

Classify a Flow by what starts it

↻
COMMONRecord-Triggered FlowA Flow that runs automatically when a record is created, updated, or in supported scenarios deleted. Click to open the glossary.

Runs because a Salesforce record changes.

◷
COMMONScheduled FlowA Flow that runs at configured times instead of waiting for a user to edit a record. Click to open the glossary.

Runs at a defined time or schedule.

▤
COMMONScreen FlowAn interactive Flow that guides a user through one or more screens. Click to open the glossary.

Runs interactively with a user.

⚙
REUSABLEAutolaunched FlowA Flow without screens that is usually invoked by another automation or Apex. Click to open the glossary.

Runs when another process calls it.

⚡
EVENT DRIVENPlatform Event FlowA Flow that responds to a Salesforce platform event, often in integration-oriented designs. Click to open the glossary.

Runs in response to a platform event.

◎
COORDINATIONFlow OrchestratorA Salesforce capability for coordinating longer multi-step processes across flows, approvals, and people. Click to open the glossary.

Coordinates longer processes involving multiple steps and participants.

02
UNDERSTAND

Use the trigger to identify the Flow type

Customer wordingLikely Flow typeWhy
“Whenever I save this Opportunity…”Record-Triggered

The record change starts the automation.

“Every morning at 8…”Scheduled

No record edit is required at that moment.

“The wizard asks me several questions…”Screen Flow

The process requires direct user interaction.

“Another Flow calls this reusable automation…”Autolaunched

Another process invokes it.

Identify scope before you inspect details

RECORDCreated / updated / deleted

Verify the record-trigger conditions and whether the record met them.

TIMEScheduled execution

Verify schedule, target records, and what should run at that time.

USERInteractive screens

Verify input, navigation, decisions, and the user path.

CALLERInvoked automation

Identify what called the autolaunched Flow and what inputs it passed.

Training context

06.6 · LEARNING TOPIC

Subflows & Flow Versions

Subflows keep automation reusable, while Flow versions preserve prior configurations. Both are critical when behavior changes after a deployment or update.

REUSE & CHANGE
01
LEARN

Keep automation modular and version-aware

SUBFLOW
Parent Flow

Main business process

↓
SubflowA reusable Flow called from another Flow so shared logic can remain modular. Click to open the glossary.

Reusable automation

↓
Return to parent

Continue the larger process

FLOW VERSIONS
v1

Earlier configuration

→
v2

Previously working version

→
v3

ACTIVE
Current runtime behavior

Only the active version controls current execution. Earlier versions are useful comparison points.

02
UNDERSTAND

Separate reuse from runtime behavior

REUSESubflows reduce duplication

A larger process can call shared automation rather than rebuilding the same logic.

ACTIVE VERSIONOnly one version drives current behavior

Do not debug an inactive version and assume it explains the customer symptom.

CHANGE COMPARISONOld vs new is evidence

When behavior changed after an update, compare the active version with the last known-good version.

DEPENDENCYCalled subflows must also succeed

Verify referenced subflows are active and completing as expected.

03
INVESTIGATE

Use version comparison as a change detector

1Confirm active version

Identify exactly what Salesforce is running now.

2Find last known-good

Use the version that worked before the reported change.

3Compare changes

Focus on elements, conditions, resources, or calls that changed.

4Verify subflows

Confirm every referenced subflow is active and completes successfully.

APPLY

Confirm the active version, compare it with the last version that created tasks correctly, and inspect any changed branch or subflow call before changing production logic.

06.8 · LEARNING TOPIC

Validation Rules

Validation Rules protect data quality by blocking a save when a configured formula evaluates to TRUE. The fastest investigation connects the formula, record values, and the process attempting the save.

DATA QUALITY GATE
01
LEARN

Remember the most important rule: TRUE blocks the save

VALIDATION FORMULA

Does the invalid-data condition evaluate to TRUE?

TRUEBlock the save

Salesforce displays the configured error message because the invalid condition was met.

FALSEAllow the save to continue

The rule does not block the transaction, though other automation or validation may still apply.

02
UNDERSTAND

Validation can affect more than a manual user save

👤
Manual save

A user editing a record can hit the rule.

⚙
Flow

A Flow record operation can fail when the target data violates the rule.

</>
Apex

DMLData Manipulation Language operations such as insert, update, and delete change Salesforce records. Click to open the glossary. in custom code can be blocked by validation.

⇧
Imports

Bulk or import tools must satisfy the same validation conditions.

Error message quality matters

A useful Validation Rule error should tell the user what data needs to change, not only that the save failed.

03
INVESTIGATE

Turn a save failure into a formula question

1Identify the rule

Which Validation Rule evaluated during the save?

2Read the formula

What condition makes the formula return TRUE?

3Inspect actual values

Which record values satisfied that invalid-data condition?

4Identify the caller

Was the save initiated manually, by Flow, Apex, or an import?

04
APPLY

Explain why the transaction was blocked

PRACTICE SCENARIO

A Flow Update Records element fails with a Validation Rule error.

Do not treat the Flow element as the root cause automatically. Identify the Validation Rule, evaluate its formula against the record values the Flow attempted to save, and determine why the invalid condition became TRUE.

Flow tries to save→Validation formula→TRUE→Save blocked

09.6 · LEARNING TOPIC

Evidence & Hypothesis

Move from facts to a hypothesis, then test it with configuration, data, logs, timeline, and comparisons.

EVIDENCE DRIVEN
01
LEARN

Do not jump from symptom to conclusion

1Facts

What is directly observed?

→
2Hypothesis

What could explain it?

→
3Test

What evidence would support or reject it?

→
4Conclusion

What does the validated evidence prove?

02
UNDERSTAND

Use evidence types that answer different questions

01Configuration

What Salesforce is configured to do.

02Data

Values and relationships actually stored.

03Logs

What executed and where it failed.

04Timeline

What changed around the symptom.

05Comparison

Working versus failing users, records, environments, or releases.

03
INVESTIGATE

Make the hypothesis testable

Hypothesis: “Permissions are blocking the save.”

SupportsSame record succeeds for a user with the required access.RejectsEquivalent effective access exists and runtime evidence shows a validation failure.
04
APPLY

Treat timing as a clue, not proof

PRACTICE SCENARIO

A save starts failing after a Flow was activated.

Use runtime evidence, record values, validation results, and comparison with the prior working configuration before assigning root cause to Flow.

05
CHECK

Confirm the core idea

QUICK CHECK

1. What comes before a technical conclusion?

2. What is timeline evidence?

Complete the quiz to finish this topic.
09.7–09.8 · LEARNING TOPIC

Pattern Recognition & Root Cause Analysis

Recognize shared patterns, then prove the underlying cause with a causal chain.

PATTERN → CAUSE
01
LEARN

Use patterns to broaden the investigation, then use RCA to explain why

PATTERN RECOGNITION

Look beyond one case

Multiple customers, a sudden volume increase, or shared release, product, edition, integration, Flow, managed package, or configuration can reveal a systemic pattern.

ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS

Explain the underlying cause

RCA defines the issue and impact, collects evidence, identifies contributing factors and causal chain, validates the cause, and documents the resolution or corrective action.

02
UNDERSTAND

Connect the pattern to a validated causal chain

1Symptom

What failed?

→
2Pattern

Who else is affected and what is shared?

→
3Evidence

What proves the common factor?

→
4Root cause

Why did the system reach the failing state?

→
5Action

Resolution, workaround, or corrective action.

03
INVESTIGATE

Do not confuse correlation with cause

01Cluster

Multiple similar cases are a clue.

02Shared variable

Identify release, product, configuration, or integration.

03Causal proof

Show how that variable creates the symptom.

04RCA

Document why the system reached the failing state.

04
APPLY

Use the cluster to guide RCA, not replace it

PRACTICE SCENARIO

Several customers report the same failure after the same release window.

The pattern justifies a broader investigation. Validate the shared release, product, configuration, and runtime evidence before stating the root cause.

05
CHECK

Confirm the core idea

QUICK CHECK

1. What can a cluster of similar cases indicate?

2. What is the difference between an exception and RCA?

3. Why combine pattern recognition with RCA?

Complete the quiz to finish this topic.
09.9 · LEARNING TOPIC

Escalation Readiness

Escalate with enough evidence and context for the receiving team to act without repeating basic discovery.

ACTIONABLE HANDOFF
01
LEARN

The next team should be able to act immediately

CORE IDEA

Escalation quality is investigation quality

Document the symptom, scope, business impact, reproduction, expected and actual behavior, logs, queries, configuration findings, ruled out paths, existing issue search, and the exact help needed.

01Symptom

Observable behavior.

02Scope

Users, records, orgs, environments.

03Impact

Business consequence.

04Reproduction

Steps and timestamps.

05Evidence

Logs, queries, configuration.

06Ask

Specific help or decision needed.

02
UNDERSTAND

Move from context to actionable handoff

1Context

Symptom, scope, impact.

→
2Evidence

Reproduction, logs, queries, configuration.

→
3Research

Known Issues and defects checked.

→
4Ask

Exact decision or engineering help needed.

03
INVESTIGATE

Check whether basic discovery is still missing

01Reproducible?

Can another engineer follow the same steps?

02Evidence visible?

Are logs and findings attached or summarized?

03Ruled out?

Can they see what has already been tested?

04Specific ask?

Is the needed help explicit?

04
APPLY

Do not use escalation as a substitute for investigation

PRACTICE SCENARIO

You suspect a product defect but have no reproduction steps or logs.

Continue collecting evidence and search for existing work before escalating. The receiving team should not need to ask the same basic discovery questions.

05
CHECK

Confirm the core idea

QUICK CHECK

1. What makes an escalation ready?

2. What should be explicit in the escalation?

09.10 · LEARNING TOPIC

Swarming

Bring additional expertise into the investigation while keeping ownership and context clear.

COLLABORATE WITH CONTEXT
01
LEARN

Ask for help with enough context to contribute immediately

CORE IDEA

Swarming adds expertise without unnecessary transfers

A strong Swarm Request summarizes the customer experience, work already completed, evidence collected, and the specific help requested.

01Customer experience

What is happening?

02Work completed

What has been investigated?

03Evidence

What logs, tests, or facts matter?

04Ask

What expertise or confirmation is needed?

02
UNDERSTAND

Keep collaboration focused and owned

01Clear owner

One engineer maintains the case path.

02Focused communication

Keep the conversation useful to the investigation.

03Cross cloud collaboration

Bring in another product area before transferring when appropriate.

04Close deliberately

End the swarm when collaboration is genuinely complete.

03
INVESTIGATE

Make the request answerable in one read

STRONG SWARM REQUEST

Symptom: what the customer sees. Evidence: what has been tested. Scope: who and what is affected. Ask: the expertise or decision needed.

04
APPLY

Use a swarm when expertise is needed but ownership does not need to move

PRACTICE SCENARIO

A Service Cloud case appears to involve a Sales Cloud automation dependency.

Bring the relevant expertise into the investigation with the existing evidence and a specific question before transferring ownership unnecessarily.

05
CHECK

Confirm the core idea

QUICK CHECK

1. What belongs in a strong Swarm Request?

2. Does swarming automatically transfer ownership?

09.11 · LEARNING TOPIC

Release Readiness

Distinguish expected product change, regression, and unrelated customer configuration during release windows.

RELEASE CONTEXT
01
LEARN

Treat “it started after the release” as a clue

CORE IDEA

Compare versions before declaring a regression

Review release schedules, release notes, pre release orgs, release Known Issues, internal release channels, and the same behavior across versions.

02
UNDERSTAND

Use the release lifecycle as an evidence framework

1Before

Review schedule, release notes, pre release behavior.

→
2During

Watch Known Issues, channels, and case patterns.

→
3After

Compare versions and prove what changed.

03
INVESTIGATE

Separate timing from causation

01Release notes

Was the change intentional?

02Known Issues

Is the symptom already documented?

03Version comparison

Does the same path behave differently?

04Customer changes

Could local configuration explain the timing?

04
APPLY

Prove the release relationship before calling it a regression

PRACTICE SCENARIO

The customer says the feature failed immediately after the seasonal release.

Compare the same path across versions, review release notes and Known Issues, and check customer changes. Release timing alone is not root cause.

05
CHECK

Confirm the core idea

QUICK CHECK

1. How should “it started after the release” be treated?

2. What helps prove a regression?

09.12 · LEARNING TOPIC

Final Investigation Checklist

Verify that the investigation tells a complete story before resolution, transfer, or escalation.

CONSISTENCY CHECK
01
LEARN

Make the investigation reusable

01Scope

Defined.

02Impact

Severity and business context understood.

03Expected vs actual

Documented.

04Reproduction

Attempted with steps.

05Timeline

Recent changes reviewed.

06Research

Cases, Knowledge, Known Issues, and defects searched.

07Configuration & data

Validated.

08Logs & queries

Collected when needed.

09Hypotheses

Tested with evidence.

10Communication

Customer update current.

11Next action

Resolution or next step documented.

02
UNDERSTAND

A complete case answers the next engineer’s questions in order

1Problem

What is happening?

→
2Impact

Why does it matter?

→
3Evidence

What proves the behavior?

→
4Tests

What was validated or ruled out?

→
5Conclusion

What is the supported cause?

→
6Next action

What happens now?

03
INVESTIGATE

Identify what is still missing

01Not ready

Major discovery or evidence gaps remain.

02Nearly ready

Evidence exists, but the story is not connected.

03Ready

Another engineer can continue without repeating discovery.

04
APPLY

Use the checklist before the final handoff

PRACTICE SCENARIO

You have a likely cause but the case lacks reproduction steps and business impact.

Fill the missing context before closure or escalation so the investigation history remains understandable and reusable.
